name: rivertown-science
note: A small FICTIONAL scientific world in two fields (DevOps and applied mathematics): the papers, authors and numbers are invented, so that only the corpus can know the answers. It holds the traps of a real literature review: a retracted paper, papers published after the cut-off, an off-topic paper, a small study that cannot settle the question, and a question that no paper answers.

works.title: Canary releases in a mid-size web shop: a field study
works.abstract: We compare canary releases with big-bang deployment in a mid-size web shop over twelve months and 240 releases. Canary releases reduced failed releases by 38 percent.

sections.introduction: Failed releases cost the shop an estimated two engineer-days each.
sections.methods: Releases alternated between a canary stage that reached 5 percent of the users and a direct release to all users. A release counted as failed if it was rolled back within 24 hours.
sections.results: Of 120 big-bang releases 21 failed, of 120 canary releases 13 failed.
sections.conclusion: Canary releases reduced failed releases by 38 percent in this shop. We could not test whether the effect depends on the quality of monitoring.

works.title: A replication of the canary release study at three companies
works.abstract: We repeat the canary release study at three companies with 410 releases. Failed releases fell by 31 to 42 percent; the reduction was smaller at the company with the weakest monitoring.

sections.introduction: The first field study came from a single web shop, so we repeated it elsewhere.
sections.methods: Each company released with and without a canary stage in alternating periods and counted rollbacks within 24 hours.
sections.results: Company A: 42 percent fewer failed releases, company B: 38 percent, company C, which has weak monitoring: 31 percent.
sections.conclusion: Canary releases reduced failed releases at all three companies. The reduction was smaller where monitoring was poor, so monitoring quality seems to matter.

works.title: Small-team canary deployments: a pilot
works.venue: Proceedings of the Release Engineering Workshop
works.abstract: Five teams of at most six people tried canary releases for six months. The number of releases was too small for a firm conclusion.

sections.introduction: Most studies of canary releases come from large organisations.
sections.methods: Five teams of at most six people released with a canary stage for six months and compared with the six months before.
sections.results: Failed releases fell in three teams and rose in two; the differences were not significant.
sections.conclusion: With fewer than 40 releases per team we found no significant difference. We cannot say whether canary releases help small teams.

works.title: Canary deployment does not reduce failed releases: evidence from a bank
works.abstract: In the release data of a bank, canary deployment showed no effect on failed releases.

sections.methods: We analysed the release records of one bank.
sections.results: The share of failed releases was the same with and without a canary stage.
sections.conclusion: We found no reduction of failed releases through canary deployment.

retraction.reason: the release data counted rollbacks twice

works.title: Progressive exposure of releases: a survey of practices
works.abstract: We survey how organisations expose releases step by step. Most reports we found describe fewer failed releases; the best evidence comes from two field studies.

sections.introduction: Exposing a release to a small group of users first has many names.
sections.methods: We read 31 reports and field studies and sorted them by the evidence they give.
sections.results: Twenty-six reports describe fewer failed releases, five describe no change. Two field studies measure the effect.
sections.conclusion: Staged exposure of releases, of which canary releases are the best known form, is widely reported to reduce failed releases. Evidence for very small teams is missing.

works.title: Canary releases and failure rates: a meta-analysis
works.abstract: A meta-analysis of seven studies with 1,950 releases in total.

sections.introduction: Several studies of canary releases exist; their results have not been pooled.
sections.methods: We pooled the reductions of failed releases of seven studies with a random effects model.
sections.results: The pooled reduction was 35 percent with a 95 percent interval from 27 to 42 percent.
sections.conclusion: The pooled reduction of failed releases was 35 percent. The effect was weaker where monitoring was poor.

works.title: A history of the Rivertown deploy tool
works.abstract: The deploy tool of the Rivertown company, from a shell script to a service.

sections.introduction: The tool started as a shell script of forty lines.
sections.methods: We read the commit history of the tool.

works.title: The Kessler-Voss iteration for nonlinear equations
works.abstract: We introduce an iteration for scalar nonlinear equations and show that it converges quadratically near a simple root.

sections.introduction: Iterations for nonlinear equations differ in speed and in the region where they work.
sections.methods: We analyse the error of the iteration near a simple root and test it on forty equations.
sections.results: For starting values closer than 0.1 to a simple root, the error after n steps behaves like the square of the error after n-1 steps.
sections.conclusion: The iteration converges quadratically near a simple root. The convergence is local: for starting values far from a root it can fail to converge.

works.title: Behaviour of the Kessler-Voss iteration at multiple roots
works.abstract: At a root of multiplicity m of at least 2, the iteration converges only linearly.

sections.introduction: Multiple roots are known to slow down many iterations.
sections.methods: We derive the error recursion at a root of multiplicity m and confirm it numerically.
sections.results: The error is multiplied by (m-1)/m in every step.
sections.conclusion: At multiple roots the Kessler-Voss iteration loses its quadratic convergence and converges linearly with rate (m-1)/m.

works.title: Damped Kessler-Voss: restoring fast convergence at multiple roots
works.abstract: A damping factor equal to the multiplicity restores quadratic convergence; for unknown multiplicity we propose an estimate.

sections.introduction: The loss of speed at multiple roots can be repaired if the multiplicity is known.
sections.methods: We add a damping factor to the iteration and study it for known and for estimated multiplicity.
sections.results: With the factor set to m the error is squared in every step; with the estimate it is squared after a short start phase.
sections.conclusion: With the damping factor set to the multiplicity m, quadratic convergence is restored. If m is unknown, an estimate from three successive steps works in our tests.

works.title: Global convergence of the Kessler-Voss iteration
works.abstract: We prove that the iteration converges from every starting value.

sections.introduction: The convergence of the iteration is known to be local.
sections.methods: We give a proof by induction over the steps.
sections.results: The proof shows convergence for all real starting values.

works.title: The Kessler-Voss iteration in extended precision
works.abstract: We run the iteration in extended precision.

sections.introduction: Rounding limits how far an iteration can converge.
sections.methods: We repeat the experiments of the first paper with 34 digits.
sections.results: The error falls quadratically until the rounding level of 1e-34.
sections.conclusion: In extended precision the quadratic convergence near simple roots is unchanged, but rounding stops the iteration earlier than in the analysis.

works.title: Notes on bisection for monotone functions
works.abstract: Bisection halves the interval in every step.

sections.introduction: Bisection is the simplest method for a monotone function.
sections.methods: We count the steps for given accuracies.
sections.results: Thirty-four steps give ten digits on the unit interval.
sections.conclusion: Bisection needs about 3.3 steps per digit.
